rows.notes: The cited work is a narrative review with an embedded global meta-analysis (Section 4, Figure 5: 1164 comparisons from 117 publications) on yield, WP and IWP of drip versus flood, border, furrow, sprinkler and micro-sprinkler irrigation. The meta-analysis does report higher WP/IWP under drip at <100% and 100-120% application and mentions 95% CIs, but as a review/meta-analysis it is not a primary study under Q1, so Q2-Q9 are scored no by rule.

Review plus meta-analysis of other studies. Section 4.1/Figure 5 reports that with drip amount <100% of the comparison method, yield was significantly higher than flooding (95% CI 6.12-7.55%) and furrow (6.74-7.93%) but not different from border or micro-sprinkler; at 100-120% yield rose by 28.92%, 14.55%, 8.03%, 2.32%, 5.17%. No own experimental data; Q1 is no under the meta-analysis rule.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The 'water scarcity' framing in the passage corresponds to the review's synthesis statement that drip saves water and maintains yield when the drip amount is below that of other methods (Section 4.1, Figure 5); nothing in the document is a primary risk-management result.

Review/meta-analysis. The closest content is Figure 5/Section 4.1, where at <100% drip amount yield did not differ significantly from border or micro-sprinkler irrigation, which the citing text uses to argue that drip may not raise yield where water is not limiting. Not a primary study, so scored no throughout.

Review. Emitter clogging is discussed in Section 2 and 8.2 (narrow 0.5-1.2 mm channels, blockage reducing uniformity and system life) and salt accumulation at edges of wetted zones in Section 7 (Wu et al.: wide rows and intermembrane showed salt accumulation), all drawn from cited literature, not own data, and no yield reduction is measured.

Review. Section 7 summarises other studies on salt accumulation in the root zone under drip in inherently saline soils and at wide-row/intermembrane positions, but reports no own measurements; not a primary study.

Review. The description of drip fertigation delivering water and fertilizer directly to roots and reducing evaporation/seepage appears in the Introduction and Section 2 as a general characterisation citing other works; the meta-analysis addresses WP/IWP but not evaporation directly, and the document is not a primary study.
